docs.title: KeyLease
docs.text:
A Soroban protocol on Stellar that turns metered API/RPC access into time-bound, escrowed micro-leases.

KeyLease replaces long-lived static API keys with leases: expiring on-chain authorizations backed by a SEP-41 micropayment held in Soroban escrow. Providers publish a price instead of a secret; consumers pay only for the calls they use; the Stellar ledger holds the truth about every lease.

  • Repository: keylease-core — the Soroban contracts
  • License: MIT

docs.title: Architecture
docs.text: KeyLease is one Soroban contract and the Stellar ledger it runs on. There is no second source of truth: services, leases, escrow balances and lifecycle history all live on-chain, and the contract exposes them through entry points and contract events.

docs.title: KeyLeaseRegistry
docs.text:
A pure Rust Soroban contract. It is the only component that can move value.

Module Role lib.rs Entry points, contractmeta!, upgrade, lifecycle documentation. types.rs Service, Lease, LeaseStatus. storage.rs DataKey layout, instance/persistent split, duration-aware TTL policy. events.rs Typed #[contractevent] payloads for every transition. errors.rs Stable error codes (part of the ABI).

The registry is deliberately small. It does not know what an HTTP request is, what the endpoint does, or who is calling it. It knows service_id, allocated_calls, expires_at and locked_deposit.

docs.title: SEP-41 token
docs.text:
The registry holds no privileged token logic. It calls the standard SEP-41 transfer on the token configured by the admin:

  • the native Stellar Asset Contract wraps XLM (the usual Testnet choice),
  • any custom SEP-41 asset works without a contract change,
  • contracts/mock_token exists only for tests and local sandboxes.

The token boundary is a cross-contract call, so the money paths follow checks-effects-interactions and are tested against a re-entrant token.

docs.title: Consumers of the ledger
docs.text:
There is no privileged off-chain service. Anyone can observe the protocol using standard Stellar tooling:

Consumer How it reads the protocol Provider request path get_lease over Soroban RPC (cached for a short TTL), or a local projection built from the event stream. Accounting / dashboards stellar events, Horizon or an indexer subscribing to lease_created / lease_settled / lease_revoked. CLI tooling stellar contract invoke for writes and reads (reads need any funded --source-account).

See Integration for the concrete verification pipeline.

docs.title: Data flow: one metered call
docs.text:
sequenceDiagram
    participant C as Consumer
    participant R as KeyLeaseRegistry
    participant T as SEP-41 token
    participant P as Provider service
    participant U as Upstream API

    C->>R: create_lease(consumer, service_id, calls, duration)
    R->>T: transfer(consumer → registry, rate × calls)
    R-->>C: lease_id + lease_created event
    C->>P: request + Stellar-signed proof of consumer address
    P->>R: get_lease(lease_id)   (TTL-cached)
    R-->>P: Lease { allocated_calls, used_calls, expires_at, settled, ... }
    alt lease active, unexpired, quota remains
        P->>U: forwarded request
        U-->>P: response
        P-->>C: response + x-keylease-calls-remaining
    else invalid / expired / quota exhausted
        P-->>C: 401 / 403 / 429
    end
    P->>R: settle_lease(provider, lease_id, verified_calls)
    R->>T: payout + refund
    R-->>P: lease_settled event

docs.title: Why the contract is minimal
docs.text:
Every line of on-chain code is attack surface for escrowed funds. endpoint_hash is a commitment precisely so the contract never has to reason about off-chain credentials. Usage reporting is a single settlement call rather than one transaction per API call, which keeps the protocol affordable for small allotments.

Off-chain enforcement is replaceable. A provider can read leases directly over RPC, run an indexer, or write their own middleware. The protocol does not depend on any of those being alive: if a proxy is down, providers can still settle with stellar contract invoke, and consumers can still revoke.

Trust flows one way. Off-chain code trusts the ledger for lease state. The contract trusts nobody: every mutating entry point authenticates the actor it claims to represent, and the consumer always has an exit.

docs.title: Storage
docs.text:
Key Storage TTL policy Admin, Token instance extended on every state change (≈30 days) ServiceCount, LeaseCount instance same as instance Service(u64) persistent extended on save and on read (≈30 days) Lease(u64) persistent extended for the lease's remaining term plus the 24h grace window and a one-day read buffer

create_lease caps duration_secs at MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (30 days), so the TTL extension is bounded and a locked deposit can never outlive its entry. Only the time a lease can be acted on is paid for, so Soroban rent does not dominate short leases. The host still clamps TTL to its minimum persistent TTL (≈7 days on Testnet).

docs.title: Consumer guide
docs.text: You want metered access to an API or RPC endpoint without a permanent static key. This guide walks through buying, using and reclaiming a lease with Stellar.

docs.title: The deal you are getting
docs.text:
• You prepay rate_per_call × requested_calls into Soroban escrow.
  • You get an on-chain authorization that expires after duration_secs.
  • You pay only for the calls you use: unused balance is refunded at settlement.
  • If the provider never settles, you reclaim the entire deposit 24 hours after expiry — no support ticket, no trust required.

Your Stellar account is your identity. There is no API key to copy into a .env file and no separate credential service.

docs.title: 1. Pick a service
docs.text:
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account <funded-account> \
  --network testnet -- get_service --service_id 1

Returns the provider, rate_per_call, is_active and endpoint_hash. Confirm the endpoint_hash matches the endpoint descriptor the provider published off-chain before you escrow anything.

docs.title: 2. Fund your account
docs.text:
Any SEP-41 token the registry is configured with can be escrowed. On Testnet the native asset's SAC is the usual choice, and Friendbot funds accounts with 10,000 fake XLM.

# Testnet only: create + fund in one step
stellar keys generate consumer --network testnet --fund

# or fund an address you already have
curl "https://friendbot.stellar.org?addr=$(stellar keys address consumer)"

docs.title: 3. Create the lease
docs.text:
export REGISTRY=<your registry contract id>
export CONSUMER=$(stellar keys address consumer)

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- create_lease \
     --consumer $CONSUMER \
     --service_id 1 \
     --requested_calls 500 \
     --duration_secs 3600

This escrows rate_per_call × 500 and prints the new lease_id. The transaction emits lease_created { lease_id, service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit }; keep the transaction hash as proof of purchase.

Choose your numbers deliberately. If your lease expires while you still have unused calls, those calls are not usable — remaining_calls drops to 0 at expires_at. The maximum duration is 30 days (MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS). Under-buy with a generous duration, then renew, rather than over-buying with a short one.

Order of arguments matters. consumer is the first argument. This is the exact ABI; older documentation that shows service first is wrong.

docs.title: 4. Use the access
docs.text:
Tell the provider which lease backs your requests. Because the lease records your Stellar address, the provider authenticates you with a Stellar signature (SEP-10 challenge–response, or an equivalent signed challenge) and checks that you are lease.consumer. No bearer token is issued by KeyLease, and none is needed.

Concretely, for a provider that follows Integration:

  1. complete the provider's Stellar challenge with your account,
  2. send requests with your lease_id (path, query or header, as the provider documents) or let the provider resolve it from your authenticated address,
  3. read x-keylease-calls-remaining if the provider exposes it.

If you can sign for the account that owns the lease, you can use it — there is no separate credential to store or rotate. If you rotate that account, create a new lease from the new one.

docs.title: 5. Watch the lease
docs.text:
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- remaining_calls --lease_id 1

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer \
  --network testnet -- lease_status --lease_id 1

lease_status is 0 (Active), 1 (Expired) or 2 (Settled).

docs.title: 6. Get your money back
docs.text:
Normal path — automatic. When the provider settles, the unused balance is transferred back to you in the same transaction. Nothing to claim.

Provider went dark. After expires_at + 24 hours, reclaim everything:

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account consumer --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- revoke_expired_lease --consumer $CONSUMER --lease_id 1

This refunds the full locked_deposit and emits lease_revoked { lease_id, consumer, refund }. It works for a lease that was never used and for one that was partially used but never settled.

docs.title: Why you must wait 24 hours
docs.text: That window is reserved for the provider to settle legitimately. It is the provider's guarantee, and your refund is the counterweight. It is a fixed constant in the contract (SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS = 86_400).

docs.title: Refund decision table
docs.text: Lease state What happens Provider settles before/at expiry You get locked_deposit − used × rate back Provider settles after expiry within 24h Same as above Provider settles with verified_calls = 0 You get the entire deposit back Provider never settles, now ≥ expiry + 24h You revoke and get the entire deposit Provider never settles, inside the 24h window Nothing yet — wait

docs.title: Costs
docs.text:
Creating a lease and revoking one are two Soroban transactions (network fees plus the escrow transfer). There is no per-call on-chain cost — the provider settles with a single call count. Check the current fee with stellar network settings or your RPC provider.

create_lease also pays storage rent for keeping the lease entry alive through its term, the 24-hour grace window and a one-day buffer. Rent depends on duration, not call count, so a short lease with a larger allotment is cheaper per call than a long lease with a tiny one. The network enforces a minimum persistent TTL (≈7 days on Testnet), so a very short lease still pays that floor.

docs.title: Contract reference
docs.text:
KeyLeaseRegistry — the Soroban escrow and accounting contract for KeyLease. This page is generated by hand from contracts/registry/src/; treat the source as authoritative.

  • Package: keylease-registry
  • Wasm: target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm
  • Network target: Stellar (wasm32v1-none), soroban-sdk 26
  • Constants: SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS = 86_400 (24 hours), MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS = 2_592_000 (30 days)
  • Storage TTL: LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD = 17_280, LEDGER_BUMP_EXTEND = 518_400; leases extend to term + 24h grace + a 1-day buffer
  • On-chain metadata: name = KeyLeaseRegistry, version, description, repository, embedded with contractmeta!

Every state-changing entry point calls require_auth() on the actor it represents. Errors are returned as Result<_, Error>; codes are stable and never renumbered. Every money-moving path persists its effect before calling the SEP-41 token (checks-effects-interactions).

docs.title: init
docs.text:
pub fn init(env: Env, admin: Address) -> Result<(), Error>

Initialize the registry and appoint admin.

  • Caller / auth: admin must authorize.
  • Trigger: once, immediately after deploy.
  • Preconditions: the registry must not already be initialized.
  • State: sets Admin; extends instance TTL.
  • Events: registry_initialized { admin }.
  • Errors: AlreadyInitialized.
  • Notes: the admin can only call set_token and upgrade. It cannot move user funds.

docs.title: set_token
docs.text:
pub fn set_token(env: Env, admin: Address, token: Address) -> Result<(), Error>

Point the registry at the SEP-41 token used for every deposit and payout.

  • Caller / auth: admin, and admin must match the stored admin.
  • Trigger: once at setup; again only to migrate the escrow asset.
  • State: sets Token; extends instance TTL.
  • Events: escrow_token_set { admin, token }.
  • Errors: NotInitialized, Unauthorized.
  • Notes: the native Stellar Asset Contract (SAC) is the usual value. Changing the token while leases are unsettled is a migration hazard — settle first.

docs.title: upgrade
docs.text:
pub fn upgrade(env: Env, admin: Address, new_wasm_hash: BytesN<32>) -> Result<(), Error>

Install a new registry Wasm through the Soroban deployer.

  • Caller / auth: admin, and admin must match the stored admin.
  • Trigger: a released bug fix or feature, after uploading the Wasm with stellar contract upload.
  • Effects: env.deployer().update_current_contract_wasm(new_wasm_hash).
  • Events: contract_upgraded { admin, new_wasm_hash }.
  • Errors: NotInitialized, Unauthorized.
  • Notes: the contract id, storage and balances are preserved, so an upgrade must never change the DataKey layout or the meaning of stored values. See Deployment.

docs.title: register_service
docs.text:
pub fn register_service(
    env: Env,
    provider: Address,
    rate_per_call: i128,
    endpoint_hash: BytesN<32>,
) -> Result<u64, Error>

Publish a new leasable service.

  • Caller / auth: provider must authorize.
  • Trigger: when a provider lists an API or RPC endpoint.
  • Parameters:
  • rate_per_call — price per metered call in token stroops; must be > 0.
  • endpoint_hash — 32-byte commitment to the off-chain descriptor.
  • Returns: the new service_id (monotonic, starts at 1).
  • State: writes Service(service_id), increments ServiceCount, extends instance TTL.
  • Events: service_registered { service_id, provider, rate_per_call, endpoint_hash }.
  • Errors: InvalidRate, Overflow.

docs.title: set_service_active
docs.text:
pub fn set_service_active(
    env: Env,
    provider: Address,
    service_id: u64,
    is_active: bool,
) -> Result<(), Error>

Pause or resume new leases for a service.

  • Caller / auth: provider, and it must own the service.
  • Trigger: maintenance, incident response, or retirement.
  • State: updates Service(service_id).is_active.
  • Events: service_status_changed { service_id, provider, is_active }.
  • Errors: ServiceNotFound, Unauthorized.
  • Notes: existing leases stay valid and settleable. Deactivation only blocks create_lease.

docs.title: create_lease
docs.text:
pub fn create_lease(
    env: Env,
    consumer: Address,
    service_id: u64,
    requested_calls: u32,
    duration_secs: u64,
) -> Result<u64, Error>

Lock a deposit and mint a time-bound lease.

  • Caller / auth: consumer must authorize.
  • Trigger: a developer purchases metered access.
  • Preconditions: requested_calls > 0, 0 < duration_secs ≤ MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS, the service exists and is_active, and Token is set.
  • Effects: transfer(consumer → contract, rate_per_call × requested_calls).
  • Returns: the new lease_id (monotonic, starts at 1).
  • State: writes Lease(lease_id) with expires_at = ledger.timestamp() + duration_secs and a TTL covering the term plus grace; increments LeaseCount.
  • Events: lease_created { lease_id, service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit }.
  • Errors: InvalidCalls, InvalidDuration, DurationTooLong, ServiceNotFound, ServiceInactive, InvalidRate, TokenNotSet, Overflow.

docs.title: settle_lease
docs.text:
pub fn settle_lease(
    env: Env,
    provider: Address,
    lease_id: u64,
    verified_calls: u32,
) -> Result<(), Error>

Pay the provider for verified calls and refund the remainder to the consumer.

  • Caller / auth: provider, and it must own the lease's service.
  • Trigger: at or after expiry, or as soon as every allocated call is consumed.
  • Preconditions: lease exists, is not settled, verified_calls ≤ allocated_calls, the caller owns the service, and the lease has expired or verified_calls == allocated_calls.
  • Effects: persists used_calls and settled = true first, then calls transfer(contract → provider, verified_calls × rate_per_call) and transfer(contract → consumer, locked_deposit − payout).
  • Events: lease_settled { lease_id, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund }.
  • Errors: LeaseNotFound, LeaseAlreadySettled, InvalidCalls, Unauthorized, LeaseNotSettleable, TokenNotSet, Overflow.
  • Notes: zero-value transfers are skipped. Settling with verified_calls = 0 is a legitimate way for a provider to refund an unusable lease. A re-entrant token sees settled = true and is rejected.

docs.title: revoke_expired_lease
docs.text:
pub fn revoke_expired_lease(
    env: Env,
    consumer: Address,
    lease_id: u64,
) -> Result<(), Error>

Reclaim the full deposit when the provider never settled.

  • Caller / auth: consumer, and it must be the lease's consumer.
  • Trigger: after expires_at + SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS.
  • Effects: persists settled = true first, then transfer(contract → consumer, locked_deposit).
  • Events: lease_revoked { lease_id, consumer, refund }.
  • Errors: LeaseNotFound, Unauthorized, LeaseAlreadySettled, LeaseNotExpired, RevokeWindowNotElapsed, TokenNotSet, Overflow.
  • Notes: this is the consumer's escape hatch, and the reason escrow is safe against an unresponsive provider.

docs.text:

docs.text:
pub struct Service {
    pub service_id: u64,
    pub provider: Address,
    pub rate_per_call: i128,
    pub is_active: bool,
    pub endpoint_hash: BytesN<32>,
}

docs.title: Storage layout
docs.text:
pub enum DataKey {
    Admin,        // instance
    Token,        // instance
    ServiceCount, // instance
    LeaseCount,   // instance
    Service(u64), // persistent
    Lease(u64),   // persistent
}

#[contracttype] enums encode as a SCV_VEC whose first element is an SCV_SYMBOL variant name — so DataKey::Lease(7) is the wire key Vec[Symbol("Lease"), u64(7)]. This matters if you read contract data directly with getContractData; see the developer guide.

docs.title: Error codes
docs.text:
Codes are part of the ABI. New variants are appended; existing numbers are never reused.

Code Variant Meaning 1 AlreadyInitialized init called twice 2 NotInitialized registry has no admin 3 Unauthorized caller is not the required actor 4 ServiceNotFound no service with that id 5 ServiceInactive service is paused 6 LeaseNotFound no lease with that id 7 LeaseAlreadySettled lease already settled or revoked 8 LeaseNotSettleable not expired and not fully consumed 9 LeaseNotExpired revoke before expiry 10 RevokeWindowNotElapsed revoke inside the 24h grace window 11 InvalidCalls zero calls, or more than allocated 12 InvalidDuration zero duration 13 InvalidRate non-positive rate 14 TokenNotSet escrow token not configured 15 Overflow checked arithmetic failed 16 DurationTooLong lease duration above MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS

docs.title: MockToken (test only)
docs.text:
contracts/mock_token implements a minimal SEP-41 surface — init, mint, transfer, transfer_from, approve, allowance, balance, decimals (7), name, symbol, admin — with an unlimited mint.

It exists so local sandboxes do not depend on a live SAC, but it must never be deployed to a network holding value. The registry's own tests escrow against the real Stellar Asset Contract (register_stellar_asset_contract_v2).

docs.title: Deployment
docs.text:
Deploying KeyLease is a short, strictly ordered sequence of stellar contract commands against a Stellar network. Steps 2–5 each depend on the previous one, so the whole thing is scripted:

SOURCE_ACCOUNT=keylease-admin ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh

To create and fund the identity as well (Testnet only):

KEYLEASE_GENERATE_KEY=1 SOURCE_ACCOUNT=keylease-admin ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh

The script never deploys mock_token. That token has an unlimited mint and is for tests and local sandboxes only.

docs.title: What the script does
docs.text:
1. cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --all
2. stellar contract deploy   <registry wasm>  -> REGISTRY contract id
3. stellar contract invoke -- init            --admin  <ADMIN>
4. stellar contract invoke -- set_token       --admin <ADMIN> --token <TOKEN>
5. stellar contract invoke -- register_service --provider <P> \
                              --rate_per_call <R> --endpoint_hash <H>

Then it re-reads get_service to confirm the write landed, and prints a block you can paste into .env:

KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID=C...
KEYLEASE_SERVICE_ID=1
KEYLEASE_TOKEN_ADDRESS=...
KEYLEASE_NETWORK=testnet
KEYLEASE_RPC_URL=https://soroban-testnet.stellar.org

docs.title: Doing it manually
docs.text:
The script is the supported path, but the raw commands are:

# 0. identity
stellar keys generate keylease-admin --network testnet --fund

# 1. build
rustup target add wasm32v1-none
cargo build --target wasm32v1-none --release --package keylease-registry

# 2. deploy
REGISTRY=$(stellar contract deploy \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet \
  --alias keylease-registry)

# 3. initialize
ADMIN=$(stellar keys address keylease-admin)
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- init --admin "$ADMIN"

# 4. configure the escrow token (native SAC here)
TOKEN=$(stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native)
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- set_token --admin "$ADMIN" --token "$TOKEN"

# 5. publish a service
stellar contract invoke --id "$REGISTRY" --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- register_service \
    --provider "$ADMIN" \
    --rate_per_call 1000000 \
    --endpoint_hash 0707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707070707

--send=yes is required for the state-changing invocations. Without it the CLI only simulates. The -- before the function name is required.

docs.title: Upgrading
docs.text:
The contract is upgradeable in place through the Soroban deployer; the contract id, storage and balances are preserved.

# 1. upload the new Wasm and print its hash
WASM_HASH=$(stellar contract upload \
  --wasm target/wasm32v1-none/release/keylease_registry.wasm \
  --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet)

# 2. install it (admin auth)
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet --send=yes -- upgrade \
    --admin $ADMIN --new_wasm_hash "$WASM_HASH"

# 3. confirm the new version and watch the event
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin --network testnet -- version
stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>

Or use the script:

REGISTRY=C... SOURCE_ACCOUNT=keylease-admin ./scripts/deploy-testnet.sh --upgrade

Guard rails for an upgrade: keep the storage layout unchanged, append error codes instead of renumbering, and keep event names and payload fields backwards-compatible. Settle or revoke in-flight leases before changing token semantics. See Security.

docs.title: Adding a new entry point
docs.text:
1. Add the variant(s) to errors.rs (append, never renumber).
  2. Add any new DataKey variants to storage.rs with a documented TTL policy.
  3. Implement the entry point in lib.rs, documenting auth + preconditions.
  4. Add a typed event in events.rs and publish it after the state is persisted.
  5. Add tests covering the happy path and each failure/refund path, plus the emitted event.
  6. Update the interface and event tables in README.md and docs/contract-reference.md.

docs.title: Code standards
docs.text:
• #![no_std] — no std in contract code; the target is wasm32v1-none.
  • All token math is checked; map failures to Error::Overflow.
  • Authenticate actors with require_auth() on the address you represent.
  • Follow checks-effects-interactions. Persist settled (or the equivalent) before any cross-contract call.
  • Guard money paths with the settled check first.
  • Bound storage. Every persistent key needs a TTL policy and, if user input controls its lifetime, an upper bound.
  • No unbounded loops over user-supplied collections.
  • Errors over panics.
  • Never reuse an error code.
  • Emit events for every state transition; never put secrets in one.

docs.title: Testing conventions
docs.text:
Use env.mock_all_auths() for happy paths and try_* client methods to assert specific errors:

assert_eq!(
    client.try_settle_lease(&provider, &lease_id, &11),
    Err(Ok(Error::InvalidCalls))
);

Event tests compare the emitted topics and payload with the event type generated by #[contractevent]:

assert_single_event(
    &env,
    &registry_id,
    &LeaseSettled { lease_id, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund },
);

The suite also deploys the real Stellar Asset Contract as the escrow token (env.register_stellar_asset_contract_v2), and installs a hostile SEP-41 token that re-enters settle_lease to prove the double-settlement guard holds. Keep both patterns when adding money paths.

Every security-sensitive change needs an adversarial test — an attempt to steal, strand, or double-spend.

  • Bump the workspace version so version() and contractmeta! change.

Clients should prefer the read views and the event stream over raw storage:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1
stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger 123456

If you must read storage directly, #[contracttype] enums encode as an SCV_VEC whose first element is an SCV_SYMBOL with the variant name:

Logical key Wire key DataKey::Admin Symbol("Admin") DataKey::Lease(7) Vec[Symbol("Lease"), u64(7)] DataKey::Service(3) Vec[Symbol("Service"), u64(3)]

With @stellar/stellar-sdk:

import { xdr, nativeToScVal } from '@stellar/stellar-sdk';

// DataKey::Lease(leaseId)
xdr.ScVal.scvVec([
  xdr.ScVal.scvSymbol('Lease'),
  nativeToScVal(leaseId, { type: 'u64' }),
]);

getContractData returns a scvMap of the Lease struct fields. Decode it as { lease_id, service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, used_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit, settled }. Full details are in the contract reference, and the supported way to verify leases is described in Integration.

docs.title: Integration
docs.text:
KeyLease has no privileged off-chain service and no bespoke credential format. A provider integrates with the Stellar ledger directly: it verifies the lease on chain, binds the caller to the lease's consumer using Stellar account authentication, and settles through the contract.

This page describes the supported pattern. Any implementation that follows it is compatible with the protocol.

docs.title: What the credential is
docs.text:
The lease is the credential. get_lease(lease_id) returns the authoritative terms: allocated_calls, used_calls, expires_at, settled, and the consumer who owns the refund path. A provider admits a request only when that on-chain record says it is allowed.

There is nothing else to issue: no API key, no session JWT, no signing secret. The consumer's identity is its Stellar address (G… or C…).

docs.title: The verification pipeline
docs.text:
A provider should implement these steps, in order, and fail closed at every one:

  1. Authenticate the caller with Stellar. Use a challenge–response flow with the consumer's Stellar key; SEP-10 Stellar Web Authentication is the standard way to prove account ownership to an off-chain service. The result is a trusted Address for the request — not a password.
  2. Resolve the lease on chain. Call get_lease(lease_id) over Soroban RPC and cache the result briefly (a few seconds is usually enough for a busy provider). An unreachable RPC is a 503, never an allow.
  3. Check the lease. The lease must exist, must not be settled, and ledger.timestamp() < expires_at. Reject otherwise (403).
  4. Check ownership. The authenticated address must equal lease.consumer. Otherwise reject (403). This is what makes a stolen lease id worthless.
  5. Enforce the quota. Use max(lease.used_calls, local_counter) against lease.allocated_calls; reject with 429 when exhausted, and increment the counter only for admitted requests.
  6. Serve the request, adding the remaining-calls header if you want the client to see its budget.
  7. Settle with settle_lease when the lease expires or when the allotment is fully consumed.

Step 5's local counter is an optimisation, not the source of truth. On-chain allocated_calls × rate_per_call bounds what the provider can ever be paid, so a tampered counter can only make the provider charge less. It can never over-charge the consumer.

docs.title: Reading a lease
docs.text:
With the Stellar CLI:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account keylease-admin \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1

With @stellar/stellar-sdk, simulate a get_lease invocation and decode the result:

import {
  Contract, TransactionBuilder, Networks, Account,
  nativeToScVal, scValToNative, rpc,
} from '@stellar/stellar-sdk';

const server = new rpc.Server(process.env.KEYLEASE_RPC_URL!);
const contract = new Contract(process.env.KEYLEASE_CONTRACT_ID!);

export async function readLease(leaseId: bigint) {
  const source = new Account(
    'GAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAAWHF',
    '0',
  );
  const tx = new TransactionBuilder(source, {
    fee: '100',
    networkPassphrase: Networks.TESTNET,
  })
    .addOperation(contract.call('get_lease', nativeToScVal(leaseId, { type: 'u64' })))
    .setTimeout(30)
    .build();

  const sim = await server.simulateTransaction(tx);
  if (!rpc.Api.isSimulationSuccess(sim) || !sim.result) {
    throw new Error('get_lease failed');
  }
  return scValToNative(sim.result.retval) as {
    lease_id: bigint;
    service_id: bigint;
    consumer: string;
    allocated_calls: number;
    used_calls: number;
    expires_at: bigint;
    locked_deposit: bigint;
    settled: boolean;
  };
}

The read views require no authorization, so simulation is enough — a provider never needs a Stellar secret key to verify a lease. That is deliberate: compromising an enforcement tier does not compromise escrowed funds.

docs.title: Following the event stream
docs.text:
For accounting, dashboards and settlement automation, subscribe to the contract's events instead of polling every lease:

stellar events --id $REGISTRY --network testnet --start-ledger <ledger>
Event Use lease_created Build a work queue of leases to settle; alert on new demand. lease_settled Reconcile payouts and refunds; close the lease in your ledger. lease_revoked A consumer reclaimed an expired lease; the provider earned nothing. service_registered / service_status_changed Keep a service catalogue in sync. contract_upgraded Detect a new Wasm version (version() also changes).

Every event carries the ids as topics, so a subscriber can filter by lease_id or service_id without decoding the payload. Event names and fields are part of the ABI; see the contract reference.

docs.title: Settling
docs.text:
Settlement is one signed transaction from the provider account, at or after expiry, or as soon as every allocated call is consumed:

stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- settle_lease \
    --provider $PROVIDER --lease_id 1 --verified_calls 320

Reporting verified_calls = 0 refunds the entire deposit for a lease you could not serve. Choose a settlement cadence that fits your traffic: one settlement per lease, not per request.

docs.title: Hardening checklist
docs.text:
• [ ] Verify leases server-side; never trust a lease_id supplied by the client without checking consumer against an authenticated Stellar address.
  • [ ] Fail closed on RPC errors, malformed lease data and unknown leases.
  • [ ] Cache lease reads briefly (≈5–30 s) but never past the request you are authorising; re-read on a cache miss or when close to expires_at.
  • [ ] Share the per-lease counter if you run more than one instance, or accept that each instance can grant the full allotment (the provider only loses revenue; the consumer is still bounded on chain).
  • [ ] Keep provider signing keys out of the request path where possible: reads need no key, only settlement does.
  • [ ] Watch lease_created so no lease expires unsettled and becomes revocable.
  • [ ] Never log Stellar secret seeds.

docs.title: The problem
docs.text:
Every API and RPC provider on Stellar hands out the same artifact: a static API key. That credential is a liability on both sides of the relationship.

For developers, it is a secret that lives forever in a .env file. It leaks through committed repositories, CI logs, screenshots and shared machines, and because it never expires, a leak is a permanent leak. Rotating it breaks every consumer at once.

For providers, a static key means an all-or-nothing relationship. You cannot sell 1,000 calls to someone; you either grant unlimited access, or you build and operate your own billing, quota and revocation infrastructure. Usage cannot be metered on-chain, so nobody can prove what was consumed.

docs.title: The idea
docs.text:
KeyLease turns metered access into a lease, and puts the lease on Stellar.

A consumer locks a SEP-41 micropayment in Soroban escrow and receives an on-chain authorization for a fixed allotment of calls. The provider verifies the lease against Stellar instead of trusting a password, settles once with a verified call count, and is paid from escrow. Unused balance refunds automatically.

consumer                         registry                        provider
   |                                |                                |
   |-- create_lease(calls, secs) -->|                                |
   |   (escrow = rate * calls)      |                                |
   |<-- lease_id ------------------ |                                |
   |                                |                                |
   |                                |<-- settle_lease(used_calls) ---|
   |<-- refund of unused ---------- |---- payout of used ----------->|
   |                                |                                |

Two properties fall out of this design that a static key cannot offer:

  1. The credential expires on its own. Authorization is bounded by expires_at, read from ledger time. There is nothing to rotate and nothing to leak permanently.
  2. Nobody can strand your money. If the provider never settles, the consumer reclaims the entire deposit 24 hours after expiry. That refund path is what makes escrow safe to use against a provider you have never met.

docs.title: Why this is a Stellar protocol
docs.text:
KeyLease is not an off-chain SaaS that happens to store a hash on a chain. The ledger is the system of record and each part of the design maps to a Stellar primitive:

Requirement Stellar primitive Hold and move the payment SEP-41 token; the native Stellar Asset Contract (SAC) wraps XLM Prove who created or settled a lease Address authorization; accounts (G…) and contracts (C…) both work, including Stellar multisig Know when a lease expires Ledger timestamp, not an operator's clock Prove what happened Typed Soroban contract events (lease_created, lease_settled, …) Keep escrow claimable Persistent-storage TTL, extended per lease for its term + grace window Identify the deployed code contractmeta! (name, version, description, repository) and version() Fix a deployed bug upgrade(admin, new_wasm_hash) through the Soroban deployer

The consumer's proof of access is the lease itself. A provider reads it from Soroban RPC (or follows the event stream) and binds the caller to the lease's consumer address using Stellar signatures — no second credential format is invented. See Integration.

docs.title: What KeyLease is not
docs.text:
• Not a payment processor. It moves a SEP-41 token between a consumer, a provider, and escrow. It does not touch fiat.
  • Not an HTTP service. The contract cannot see your traffic. Quota checking and request forwarding are the provider's job; the on-chain lease bounds what any implementation may charge.
  • Not a credential store. Providers publish endpoint_hash, a commitment to their off-chain endpoint descriptor. No secret is ever written on-chain.

docs.title: Where it fits in the Stellar ecosystem
docs.text:
Stellar's Soroban runtime makes this practical: sub-cent fees, ~5 second ledger close, and native SEP-41 tokens mean a lease can be created, settled and refunded cheaply enough to be worth doing for small allotments of calls.

KeyLease targets a specific gap: metered API/RPC credential leasing. Adjacent Stellar escrow projects focus on milestone-based work and P2P rental escrow. Metered access — a fixed number of calls that expires — is the white space this protocol occupies.

docs.title: Escrow asset: the native SAC
docs.text:
On Testnet the usual escrow asset is the native Stellar Asset Contract for XLM. Its address is derived from the network passphrase, not invented:

stellar contract id asset --network testnet --asset native

Any SEP-41 token can be configured instead with set_token; the derive command above is only for the native asset. The admin must call set_token before any lease can be created (TokenNotSet otherwise).

docs.title: Funding accounts
docs.text:
Friendbot funds accounts and contracts with 10,000 fake XLM on Testnet:

stellar keys generate consumer --network testnet --fund
# or, for an address you already have:
curl "https://friendbot.stellar.org?addr=$(stellar keys address consumer)"

The CLI's --fund flag and the HTTP endpoint above are Testnet-only; Mainnet requires real XLM for fees and for the escrowed asset.

docs.text:
Testnet resets wipe all ledger entries, including the deployed contract, services and leases, 2–4 times per year at 17:00 UTC.

After a reset, the contract id changes. Re-run scripts/deploy-testnet.sh and update docs/deployments.md.

docs.title: RPC production notes
docs.text:
• Testnet and Futurenet public RPCs are rate-limited. They are fine for demos and reads, not for a busy provider.
  • For production, use an authenticated RPC provider and pass its URL through KEYLEASE_RPC_URL.
  • A provider's verification path fails closed when RPC is unreachable: it must reject requests rather than admit unverified ones. No funds move either way, and settlement/revocation remain possible directly through the contract.

docs.title: Actors
docs.text:
Actor Address Can do Admin one Stellar account init once, set_token, upgrade. Cannot move escrowed funds. Provider per service (account or contract address) Register/pause services, settle leases it owns. Consumer per lease (account or contract address) Create leases, revoke expired unsettled leases.

The admin is a deployment role. It can point the registry at a token address and install a new Wasm, and nothing else. It has no path to user funds.

Because every actor is a Soroban Address, the same protocol works for classic Stellar accounts (G…), multisig accounts and smart contracts (C…).

docs.title: Service
docs.text:
pub struct Service {
    pub service_id: u64,
    pub provider: Address,
    pub rate_per_call: i128,   // smallest unit of the escrow token
    pub is_active: bool,
    pub endpoint_hash: BytesN<32>,
}

A service is not an endpoint URL and not a credential. It is a price and a commitment. endpoint_hash is a 32-byte digest of the provider's off-chain descriptor, so the on-chain record proves what the endpoint should be without publishing anything secret.

docs.title: Lease
docs.text:
pub struct Lease {
    pub lease_id: u64,
    pub service_id: u64,
    pub consumer: Address,
    pub allocated_calls: u32,
    pub used_calls: u32,
    pub expires_at: u64,       // unix seconds, ledger time
    pub locked_deposit: i128,  // rate_per_call * allocated_calls
    pub settled: bool,
}

docs.title: Lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> Active: create_lease<br/>(escrow rate × calls)
    Active --> Expired: now ≥ expires_at
    Active --> Settled: settle_lease<br/>(verified_calls == allocated_calls)
    Expired --> Settled: settle_lease<br/>(provider, within grace)
    Expired --> Settled: revoke_expired_lease<br/>(consumer, after 24h grace)
    Settled --> [*]

lease_status derives the state from settled and expires_at:

Status Discriminant Condition Active 0 not settled, now < expires_at Expired 1 not settled, now ≥ expires_at Settled 2 settled == true

Discriminants are stable on the wire. They will never be renumbered.

docs.title: When can a lease be settled?
docs.text:
settle_lease reverts with LeaseNotSettleable unless either:

  • the lease has expired (now ≥ expires_at), or
  • verified_calls == allocated_calls.

The second clause is the "consumer got what it paid for" fast path: if every allocated call was consumed, the provider should not have to wait for expiry to be paid.

docs.title: The 24-hour grace window
docs.text:
After expiry there is a 24-hour window (SETTLE_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS = 86_400) during which only the provider can settle. Once it elapses, the consumer may call revoke_expired_lease and reclaim the entire deposit.

expires_at ────────────────────┬─────────────────────────────┬──────────────▶ time
                               │                             │
                        expiry reached              expires_at + 24h
                               │                             │
        provider may settle for the whole window    consumer may revoke
                               │                             │
                        ───────┴──── provider grace ─────────┘

Why a grace window at all? Without it, a provider that was offline for a minute at expiry would lose a legitimate payout to a consumer racing to revoke. The window gives providers a guaranteed settlement period while keeping the consumer's exit bounded at 24 hours.

docs.title: Events
docs.text:
Every transition publishes a typed Soroban event. Event names are the first topic, followed by the id fields marked #[topic]; the payload is a map of the remaining fields.

Event Topics Data registry_initialized — admin escrow_token_set — admin, token service_registered service_id provider, rate_per_call, endpoint_hash service_status_changed service_id provider, is_active lease_created lease_id service_id, consumer, allocated_calls, expires_at, locked_deposit lease_settled lease_id provider, verified_calls, payout, refund lease_revoked lease_id consumer, refund contract_upgraded — admin, new_wasm_hash

Events are the indexing contract between on-chain state and off-chain systems: a provider can settle from a projection built by subscribing to lease_created, and accounting can reconcile payouts from lease_settled without polling every lease. See Integration.

docs.title: Worked economics
docs.text:
All figures use the escrow token's smallest unit (7 decimals for the native asset, so 1 XLM = 10_000_000).

Suppose a provider registers a service at rate_per_call = 1_000_000 (0.1 XLM per call), and a consumer buys 500 calls for 1 hour.

1. create_lease

required_deposit = rate_per_call × requested_calls
                 = 1_000_000 × 500
                 = 500_000_000        (50 XLM)

The registry transfers 500_000_000 from the consumer into escrow and sets expires_at = now + 3600.

2a. settle_lease after 1 hour with 320 calls consumed

payout = 1_000_000 × 320 = 320_000_000   (32 XLM to the provider)
refund = 500_000_000 − 320_000_000
       = 180_000_000                     (18 XLM back to the consumer)

2b. Provider goes dark; consumer calls revoke_expired_lease after 24h

refund = locked_deposit = 500_000_000    (50 XLM, the full deposit)

2c. Consumer burns all 500 calls in 10 minutes

settle_lease is immediately allowed (verified_calls == allocated_calls):

payout = 1_000_000 × 500 = 500_000_000   (50 XLM)
refund = 0

docs.title: Cost of the lease itself
docs.text:
Creating a lease costs one Soroban transaction (fees plus the escrow transfer). Settlement costs one more. There is no per-call on-chain cost — the provider settles with a single call count, which is what makes this cheap enough for small allotments.

The create transaction also pays Soroban storage rent for extending the lease entry through its term, the 24-hour grace window and a one-day buffer. Rent scales with the duration and the number of entries, not with the number of calls, so short leases stay cheap and the TTL is deliberately not padded to the thirty-day default.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
These must hold for every reachable state. They are asserted in tests.

  1. Conservation. For every lease, payout + refund == locked_deposit.
  2. Single release. A settled lease can never be settled or revoked again (LeaseAlreadySettled), and settled is persisted before any token call.
  3. Bounded claim. A provider can never receive more than allocated_calls × rate_per_call, and only for a service it owns.
  4. Guaranteed exit. Every lease has a consumer path to a full refund.
  5. Checked math. Deposit, payout and timestamp arithmetic abort on overflow rather than truncating.
  6. Claimable storage. A lease's persistent entry outlives its term plus the grace window (MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS = 30 days).

docs.title: Storage and lifetime
docs.text:
Key Storage Notes Admin, Token instance configuration; instance TTL is bumped on every state change ServiceCount, LeaseCount instance monotonic id counters Service(u64) persistent TTL extended on save and on read Lease(u64) persistent TTL extended on save and on read to cover term + grace

LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD = 17_280 ledgers (~1 day at 5s ledgers) and LEDGER_BUMP_EXTEND = 518_400 ledgers (~30 days). For leases, save_lease and get_lease extend to (expires_at − now + 24h) / 5s + LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD ledgers, so the escrow stays claimable for the whole lease, the provider's grace window and a one-day read buffer — without paying rent for unused storage time. The host clamps persistent TTL to its network minimum (120,960 ledgers ≈ 7 days on Testnet), so very short leases pay that floor rather than a month.

docs.title: Provider guide
docs.text: You run an API or RPC endpoint. This guide shows how to sell metered access to it with KeyLease instead of handing out a static key, using only Stellar tooling and the Soroban contract.

docs.title: What you are agreeing to
docs.text:
• You publish a price per call and a 32-byte endpoint_hash commitment.
  • Consumers escrow price × calls in a SEP-41 token before they can make a request.
  • You settle a lease once, reporting how many calls were consumed.
  • If you never settle, the consumer reclaims the full deposit 24 hours after expiry. That guarantee is what makes consumers willing to prepay.

You never publish a secret on-chain. endpoint_hash is a commitment, not a credential.

docs.title: 1. Register a service
docs.text:
export REGISTRY=<your registry contract id>
export PROVIDER=$(stellar keys address provider)

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- register_service \
     --provider $PROVIDER \
     --rate_per_call 1000000 \
     --endpoint_hash $(printf '%s' "$PROVIDER:my-api" | sha256sum | awk '{print $1}')

rate_per_call is in the escrow token's smallest unit (7 decimals for the native asset, so 1000000 = 0.1 XLM per call). The command prints the new service_id — record it.

The registration emits service_registered { service_id, provider, rate_per_call, endpoint_hash }, so your own indexer can pick it up without a separate query.

docs.title: 2. Pause or resume a service
docs.text:
stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- set_service_active --provider $PROVIDER --service_id 1 --is_active false

Deactivation blocks new leases only. Existing leases stay valid and must still be settleable — you remain obligated to settle or let them expire. The change emits service_status_changed.

docs.title: 3. Verify leases and meter calls
docs.text: The contract cannot see your HTTP traffic, so verification and metering happen in your request path. The credential is the on-chain lease; there is no session token to mint.

docs.title: Verify against Soroban RPC
docs.text:
1. Authenticate the caller as a Stellar address (SEP-10 challenge–response is the standard approach).
  2. Read the lease with get_lease(lease_id) over Soroban RPC and cache it briefly.
  3. Reject if settled, if now ≥ expires_at, if the caller is not lease.consumer, or if your counter has consumed allocated_calls.
  4. Count the call, return the response.
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider \
  --network testnet -- get_lease --lease_id 1

Reads need no secret key: a verifier can run without any signing authority.

docs.title: Or project the event stream
docs.text:
If you would rather not call RPC per request, subscribe to lease_created and keep a local table of active leases. The on-chain allocated_calls and expires_at remain the bound; your projection is an optimisation.

The full pipeline, including the Stellar SDK read example and cache guidance, is in Integration.

docs.title: 4. Settle
docs.text:
Settle when the lease expires, or immediately once the consumer has used every allocated call. One settlement covers the whole lease — never one per request.

stellar contract invoke \
  --id $REGISTRY --source-account provider --network testnet \
  --send=yes -- settle_lease --provider $PROVIDER --lease_id 1 --verified_calls 320

The registry pays you verified_calls × rate_per_call, refunds the rest to the consumer, and emits lease_settled { lease_id, provider, verified_calls, payout, refund }.

Settle with verified_calls = 0 to return the entire deposit for a lease you could not serve.

docs.title: Settling rules
docs.text: Situation Result now ≥ expires_at, any verified_calls ≤ allocated_calls settle allowed verified_calls == allocated_calls, any time settle allowed now < expires_at and verified_calls < allocated_calls LeaseNotSettleable verified_calls > allocated_calls InvalidCalls lease already settled LeaseAlreadySettled you don't own the service Unauthorized

docs.title: 5. Accounting
docs.text:
settle_lease pays you from escrow. Nothing else does. The registry never holds funds on your behalf after settlement, and there is no yield or custody to manage.

  • Revenue recognised: verified_calls × rate_per_call per settlement, published in the lease_settled event.
  • Unused consumer balance: refunded by you at settlement, or by the consumer via revoke_expired_lease after the 24h grace window.
  • Disputes: there is no dispute mechanism. The consumer's protection is the refund path; yours is the grace window. Report honestly.

docs.title: Operational notes
docs.text:
• Watch expiry. A lease you forget to settle becomes revocable 24 hours after it expires. Subscribe to lease_created and settle from that queue.
  • Changing your rate. Today you register a new service; an update entry point is a wave-medium issue. In-flight leases keep their original escrow.
  • Rotating your key. A service is bound to the registering address; key rotation/transfer is a wave-medium issue. Register from an account you can keep — a Stellar multisig account works today.
  • Upgrades. Watch contract_upgraded and check version() after a release. Storage and balances are preserved across upgrades.
  • Testnet resets wipe your service. Re-register after each reset.

docs.title: Security model
docs.text: KeyLease escrows funds on Stellar. This page states exactly what the Soroban contract guarantees, what it assumes, and what is not yet hardened. For reporting a vulnerability, see SECURITY.md.

docs.title: Trust assumptions
docs.text:
Assumption Consequence if violated The admin configures a well-behaved SEP-41 token. A malicious token contract could revert transfers and stall settlement. It cannot be paid twice: settled is persisted before the transfer, and a re-entrant token is rejected (LeaseAlreadySettled). The admin does not upgrade to a malicious Wasm. An upgrade can change the contract logic. The admin key should be cold or multisig; upgrades emit contract_upgraded. The provider reports verified_calls honestly. It can under-report (it gets paid less) but never over-report past allocated_calls. Soroban ledger time is monotonic and honest. Validity windows would be unreliable. Consumers keep their own key safe. Anyone with the consumer key can create leases that spend its balance.

The provider is explicitly untrusted in the direction that matters: it cannot take more than it is owed, and it cannot prevent the consumer's refund.

docs.title: Guarantees
docs.text:
1. The provider is paid at most allocated_calls × rate_per_call. The payout is computed from the stored rate_per_call and the lease allotment; an over-claim reverts with InvalidCalls.
  2. Only the owning provider can settle. settle_lease checks service.provider == provider after authenticating provider (Unauthorized).
  3. Only the consumer can revoke, and only after the grace window. Combined checks for ownership, expiry and elapsed grace (Unauthorized, LeaseNotExpired, RevokeWindowNotElapsed).
  4. A lease releases funds once. Every money path checks settled first, persists settled = true, and only then calls the token (LeaseAlreadySettled). Checks-effects-interactions is enforced by test_reentrant_token_cannot_settle_a_lease_twice.
  5. Overflow aborts. Deposit, payout and expiry arithmetic use checked_mul/checked_add/checked_sub and revert with Overflow.
  6. Lease durations are storage-safe. Durations above MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (30 days) revert with DurationTooLong, and the persistent entry is extended for the term plus the grace window, so escrow cannot be evicted while it is claimable.
  7. The admin cannot touch user funds. It can only call set_token and upgrade.
  8. Every mutation is authenticated. No state-changing entry point trusts its caller without require_auth().
  9. Every mutation is observable. Each transition emits a typed Soroban event with no secret material in it.

docs.title: Invariants
docs.text:
Asserted in contracts/registry/src/test.rs. The contract reference lists the exact error code for each violation.

  • payout + refund == locked_deposit for every lease.
  • A settled lease never transitions again.
  • settled is true on-chain before any value leaves the contract.
  • No lease can leave more value than was escrowed.
  • Every lease has a consumer path to a full refund, for its entire TTL.

docs.title: Threats considered
docs.text: Threat Mitigation Provider claims more calls than allocated InvalidCalls Provider settles a lease twice settled flag persisted before transfers + LeaseAlreadySettled Attacker settles someone else's lease service.provider == provider check Attacker revokes someone else's lease lease.consumer == consumer check Re-entrant token pays a lease twice checks-effects-interactions; adversarial test Provider strands funds by never settling 24h grace, then full consumer refund Consumer races the provider at expiry 24h grace window reserved for the provider Rate overflow creates a cheap lease checked_mul → Overflow Duration overflow wraps expiry checked_add → Overflow Long lease is evicted from storage DurationTooLong + duration-aware TTL extension Fake "KeyLease" contract id Only ids in Deployments are ours Silent logic change on upgrade Admin-only, emits contract_upgraded, contractmeta! exposes the version

docs.title: Known limitations
docs.text:
These are real and tracked as Drips Wave issues rather than hidden.

  • Upgrade trust. The admin can replace the contract Wasm. This is a deliberate operational capability, but it means a compromised admin key can change protocol rules. A timelock or multisig requirement is future work.
  • No provider key rotation. A service is bound to the address that registered it. Transferring a service is a wave-medium issue.
  • No rate updates. Changing rate_per_call requires registering a new service; in-flight leases keep their original escrow.
  • Settlement is a single report. The contract trusts the provider's verified_calls; it cannot independently observe HTTP usage. Consumers are protected by the fixed allotment and the refund path, not by proof of non-delivery.
  • Not audited. Do not escrow mainnet value you would be unhappy to lose.

docs.title: Deployment hygiene
docs.text:
• Only trust contract ids in docs/deployments.md.
  • The admin key should be a cold or multisig Stellar account. It can change the escrow token and upgrade the contract.
  • Verify the deployed metadata and configuration after deploy:
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet -- version
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet -- get_admin
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet -- get_token
stellar contract invoke --id $REGISTRY --source-account admin --network testnet -- get_service --service_id 1

Testnet resets (2–4 times a year, at 17:00 UTC) wipe all ledger entries and change the contract id. Redeploy after a reset. See Networks.

docs.title: Disclosure
docs.text: Report vulnerabilities privately per SECURITY.md. We will credit reporters in the release notes unless asked not to.

docs.title: keylease-core v0.1.0
docs.text:
Superseded by v0.2.1. This page records the first release as it shipped; the current interface (events, upgrade, MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS) is in the contract reference.

First public release of the KeyLease registry contract.

KeyLease replaces long-lived static API/RPC credentials with time-bound, on-chain micro-leases: a consumer locks a micropayment in Soroban escrow and receives an authorization the provider can verify cheaply, with an automatic refund path if the provider goes offline.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Escrowed micro-leases. create_lease locks rate_per_call × requested_calls in a SEP-41 token and mints a lease that expires at ledger.timestamp() + duration_secs.
  • Provider settlement. settle_lease pays the provider for verified calls and refunds the remainder to the consumer. Settleable once the lease expires or once every allocated call is consumed.
  • Guaranteed consumer exit. revoke_expired_lease reclaims the full deposit 24 hours after expiry if the provider never settled — no support ticket required.
  • Service registry. Providers publish a rate and an endpoint_hash commitment instead of a secret, and can pause new leases.
  • Checked arithmetic throughout. Deposit and payout math aborts on overflow rather than truncating into a cheaper lease or a short refund.

docs.title: keylease-core v0.2.0
docs.text:
Soroban-native hardening: events, upgrades, storage-safe leases and re-entrancy protection.

This release moves the protocol closer to the Stellar primitives it depends on. The escrow model and the public lease lifecycle are unchanged, but the contract is now observable, upgradeable and hardened against hostile SEP-41 tokens.

docs.title: Highlights
docs.text:
• Typed Soroban events. Every transition publishes a #[contractevent]: registry_initialized, escrow_token_set, service_registered, service_status_changed, lease_created, lease_settled, lease_revoked and contract_upgraded. Topics carry service_id / lease_id, so the lifecycle is indexable without polling storage.
  • On-chain metadata. contractmeta! embeds the name, version, description and repository in the Wasm, and version() returns the running version.
  • In-place upgrades. upgrade(admin, new_wasm_hash) installs a new Wasm through the Soroban deployer, preserving the contract id, storage and balances. Admin-only, and it emits contract_upgraded.
  • Checks-effects-interactions. settle_lease and revoke_expired_lease persist settled = true before calling the token. A new adversarial test installs a re-entrant token that calls back into settle_lease and asserts the second attempt is rejected.
  • TTL-safe lease durations. create_lease rejects durations above MAX_LEASE_DURATION_SECS (30 days) with the new DurationTooLong (16) error, and lease storage is extended for the term plus the 24h grace window. Escrow can no longer outlive its ledger entry.
  • Real SAC coverage. The suite now escrows through register_stellar_asset_contract_v2 — the same Stellar Asset Contract that wraps native XLM — in addition to the mock token.

docs.title: keylease-core v0.2.1
docs.text: Rent-aware lease storage. A Testnet deployment showed that extending every lease to the generic thirty-day horizon made Soroban storage rent dominate short leases: creating a 100-call, one-hour lease cost more in rent than the deposit itself. This release pays only for the storage time a lease can actually be used.

docs.title: What changed
docs.text:
• Lease TTL is term-aware. save_lease and get_lease extend a lease entry to (expires_at − now + 24h) / 5s + LEDGER_BUMP_THRESHOLD ledgers: the lease's remaining term, the provider's 24-hour grace window and a one-day read buffer.
  • No more month-long padding. A one-hour lease no longer rents thirty days of storage; the host still enforces its minimum persistent TTL (~7 days on Testnet), but the unnecessary padding is gone. A 30-day lease still gets the full term plus grace and buffer, under the network's maximum entry TTL.
  • Reads use the same policy. get_lease no longer bumps to a fixed thirty-day horizon, so a read near expiry does not silently pay a month of rent.
  • Verified on Testnet. CCEZYHUJ…TAFH62 runs this build; two leases were created, fully settled and partially settled on-chain. See Deployments.
